title: Face to face (2 and 3 John)
hook: two postcards from the elder: I'd rather not write with ink, but talk face to face

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of First John, and your line was that you may know. What idol did you name, gently? Day six hundred ninety-three.

Count the times this week you texted someone you could have called, or called someone you could have visited. No judgment; it's how a lot of life works now. Long ago, a church leader who calls himself simply the elder felt the pull the other way. Two of his notes survive in the Bible, Second and Third John, each only a page or so long. And both end with almost the same line: I have more to say, but I'd rather not say it in ink. I'd rather come and talk to you face to face.
screen: `I'D RATHER NOT WRITE IT IN INK.`

segments.voice: Second John is addressed "unto the elect lady and her children, whom I love in the truth." Nobody knows who she is. She might be a woman who hosted a church in her home. Some readers think the elect lady is a way of naming a whole congregation, with her children as its members. The note repeats the heart of First John: love one another, walk in his commandments, and be careful of teachers who deny that Jesus came in the flesh. Third John is a note to one man, "the wellbeloved Gaius," and it reads like a personal letter. There's praise for Gaius, who opened his home to traveling teachers. There's a complaint about a man named Diotrephes, "who loveth to have the preeminence among them," and who turned those same travelers away. And there's a good word for someone called Demetrius. An old church quarrel, told in a few lines. Then both notes end the same way. In the King James Bible, Second John says: "Having many things to write unto you, I would not write with paper and ink: but I trust to come unto you, and speak face to face, that our joy may be full." The Greek is even more bodily than the English. It doesn't say face to face. It says mouth to mouth, stoma pros stoma. Speak with your own mouth, close enough to hear the voice. The elder knew what ink can't carry: a tone, a hand on the shoulder, the look on someone's face when they finally understand. And that closes this week. Greater than your heart. Test the spirits. God is love. No fear in love. He first loved us. That you may know. And now, face to face. A whole week about love, ending with an elder who would rather show up in person than write it down.
screen: `THE ELECT LADY: A WOMAN, OR A CHURCH?`
`A WEEK OF LOVE, ENDING IN PERSON.`
then, large: `THAT OUR JOY MAY BE FULL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: visit someone instead of messaging. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you mostly know through a screen these days: a grandparent, an old friend, a neighbor you only wave at. Picture their face. Not their profile picture: their actual face, the way it moves when they laugh. Then, in the quiet, choose one small way to be in the same room soon. A coffee, a walk, a knock on the door. If a visit isn't possible, a call where they can hear your voice counts. If you pray, you can hold their name for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Face to face. In the elder's Greek, mouth to mouth: the joy that ink can't carry, and a visit can.
Your line: face to face. Today, swap one message for a voice or a visit, and notice one thing you'd have missed on a screen. Day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: In Christian communities, hospitality and visiting, especially of the sick, the homebound and travelers, are a traditional part of life together, and 3 John's praise of Gaius is sometimes read as a picture of that welcome.
